headings.title: Introduction to Blood Pressure
headings.content: Blood pressure represents the lateral force exerted by circulating blood against the walls of the body's arteries. This hemodynamic force is generated primarily by the rhythmic contraction of the left ventricle of the heart. Two distinct measurements define every reading. **Systolic blood pressure** measures the peak arterial pressure during ventricular contraction, while **diastolic blood pressure** records the lowest arterial pressure during ventricular relaxation between heartbeats. Clinicians record these values in millimeters of mercury, abbreviated as mmHg. Understanding this basic dynamic helps nurses interpret how effectively the cardiovascular system perfuses vital organs across various clinical settings.

headings.title: Physiology and Mechanisms of Blood Pressure Regulation
headings.content: Maintaining steady blood pressure requires continuous coordination between cardiac output and peripheral vascular resistance. Blood pressure equals cardiac output multiplied by total peripheral resistance. 1. **Cardiac Output**: The total volume of blood pumped by the heart per minute, determined by stroke volume and heart rate. 2. **Peripheral Resistance**: The opposition to blood flow determined by the diameter of blood vessels, especially small arterioles. Short-term regulation relies on neural reflexes through baroreceptors located in the carotid sinuses and aortic arch. Long-term control is managed primarily by the kidneys through the **renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system**, which regulates blood volume and sodium balance.

headings.title: Classification and Normal Ranges of Blood Pressure
headings.content:
Blood pressure categorization guides clinical diagnosis and treatment urgency. Standard adult classification divides readings into distinct categories based on both systolic and diastolic numbers. 

| Category | Systolic (mmHg) | Diastolic (mmHg) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Normal | Less than 120 | Less than 80 |
| Elevated | 120 - 129 | Less than 80 |
| Stage 1 Hypertension | 130 - 139 | 80 - 89 |
| Stage 2 Hypertension | 140 or higher | 90 or higher |

A diagnosis of hypertension requires multiple elevated readings obtained on separate clinical occasions to rule out transient anxiety or situational stress.

headings.title: Techniques for Accurate Blood Pressure Assessment
headings.content:
Accurate measurement is foundational for correct clinical decisions. Errors in technique frequently lead to misdiagnosis or inappropriate medication adjustments. 

- **Cuff Selection**: The bladder width must cover approximately 40 percent of the arm circumference, and length should enclose 80 percent.
- **Patient Positioning**: The patient should sit quietly for five minutes with feet flat on the floor, back supported, and bare arm supported at heart level.
- **Inflation and Deflation**: Inflate the cuff 30 mmHg above the estimated systolic pressure, then deflate at a steady rate of 2 to 3 mmHg per second while listening for **Korotkoff sounds**.

A cuff that is too small produces falsely elevated readings, while an oversized cuff results in falsely low values.

headings.title: Hypertension: Causes, Risk Factors, and Pathophysiology
headings.content: Hypertension is classified as either primary or secondary. **Primary hypertension** has no identifiable single medical cause, developing gradually over many years due to a complex mix of genetics, lifestyle habits, and arterial stiffness. **Secondary hypertension** results from an underlying condition, most commonly renal parenchymal disease, primary aldosteronism, or sleep apnea. Prolonged high pressure damages the endothelial lining of blood vessels, promotes accelerated atherosclerosis, and increases the workload on the myocardium, ultimately leading to left ventricular hypertrophy.

headings.title: Hypotension: Causes and Clinical Implications
headings.content: Hypotension occurs when blood pressure drops below normal limits, typically defined as a systolic reading under 90 mmHg or a diastolic under 60 mmHg. While some conditioned athletes maintain low readings without symptoms, acute hypotension deprives vital organs of oxygen and nutrients. Common causes include acute blood loss, severe dehydration, septic shock, cardiac arrhythmias, and autonomic dysfunction. A notable clinical variation is **orthostatic hypotension**, defined as a drop in systolic pressure of at least 20 mmHg or diastolic of 10 mmHg within three minutes of standing up, increasing the risk of falls and syncope.

headings.title: Pharmacological and Non-Pharmacological Management
headings.content: Managing hypertension requires a comprehensive strategy combining lifestyle modifications and targeted drug therapy. Non-pharmacological interventions include adopting the DASH diet rich in fruits and vegetables, reducing sodium intake, maintaining regular aerobic exercise, limiting alcohol consumption, and achieving weight loss. When lifestyle changes are insufficient, pharmacotherapy is initiated. Major drug classes include **thiazide diuretics**, **ACE inhibitors**, **angiotensin receptor blockers**, and **calcium channel blockers**. Nurses must monitor clients for medication side effects such as dry cough with ACE inhibitors or electrolyte imbalances with diuretics.

headings.title: Complications of Untreated Blood Pressure Disorders
headings.content: Chronic, uncontrolled hypertension exerts silent, destructive force across multiple organ systems over years. The heart suffers from increased afterload, resulting in left ventricular hypertrophy, heart failure, and coronary artery disease. In the cerebral circulation, sustained high pressure weakens arterial walls, increasing the risk of ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke. Renal damage manifests as nephriosclerosis and chronic kidney disease as delicate glomerular capillaries become scarred. Retinal vessel damage can lead to hypertensive retinopathy and eventual vision loss.

headings.title: Nursing Interventions and Patient Education
headings.content: Nurses play a vital role in preventing, detecting, and managing blood pressure disorders through direct care and structured education. Essential nursing actions include performing serial blood pressure measurements, screening high-risk individuals, and reinforcing medication adherence. Patient education must emphasize that hypertension is often asymptomatic, meaning clients should never stop taking prescribed medications simply because they feel well. Nurses also teach patients how to properly use home blood pressure monitors and maintain a written log of their daily readings to share during clinical follow-up visits.
